caution: A failure to reproduce is not a finding that the paper is wrong. It may be a failure of the attempt.

attempts.label: CRCNS:pfc-1
attempts.entry_title: Task switching in rat prefrontal and auditory cortex (Rodgers and DeWeese 2014)
attempts.summary: Every main finding held up in this data: hold-period rule encoding in mPFC (76 of 121 units) and A1 (36 of 99), its earlier onset in mPFC, weaker encoding on interference trials, the link between baseline and evoked changes, impaired performance after mPFC disruption, and the network model. The minor behavioral, posture and control claims held too. The dataset does not say which of its 2977 clusters were analysed, so the unit set comes from a table in the paper's code repository. Responsiveness recomputed from spikes gave 46 and 61 units, not 31 and 49, so the responsive-unit counts and the mPFC latency lag hold only with that table. The single-unit onset medians also depend on the code's smoother and on how nine units are counted.
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Rodgers and DeWeese (2014) on CRCNS data set pfc-1, which holds the spike times and trial tables of 55 sessions of six rats performing an auditory stimulus selection task, with units in medial prefrontal cortex and primary auditory cortex, and the data of the paper's disruption, catch-trial, video-tracking and network-model analyses. It covers behaviour, the encoding of the selection rule before the stimulus, error trials, its time course, evoked responses and decoding, head posture, mPFC disruption and the model. The units analysed and their auditory response windows come from the paper's code repository.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Rodgers and DeWeese (2014) from CRCNS pfc-1

outcomes.statement: The unit and session tables of the paper's code (metadata/unit_db.csv and metadata/sessions_df.csv of github.com/cxrodgers/Rodgers2014 at commit 390b608) match the data set's spike files and session folders, and the matched units have the paper's counts per region.
outcomes.source: Experimental Procedures, link to the analysis code; the code's README (only units listed in unit_db.csv with include True were analyzed)
outcomes.notes: All 220 units with include True in unit_db.csv have spikes in their session's klusters0 spike file, 121 mPFC and 99 A1. The region column agrees with the data descriptor's unit-number rule for all 220. All 55 sessions of sessions_df.csv are session folders of the data set, and each session's n_trials equals its trial_timings rows less munged trials (55 of 55). The spike files hold 2977 clusters, 2616 of which unit_db.csv does not list.

outcomes.statement: Trained rats perform significantly above 50% correct in both localization and pitch discrimination blocks in the recording sessions, with a median of 698 trials per session; the best rats reach about 85% in both blocks. Sessions not above 50% in either block (4 of 55) were discarded.
outcomes.source: Results, A Novel Behavioral Task for Rodents, paragraph 2; Figure 2A; Supplemental Experimental Procedures, Chance performance on the task
outcomes.quote: Trained rats performed many trials per session (median, 698). We verified that the rats were performing significantly above 50% in both blocks ... Our best rats' typical performance during recording sessions was approximately 85% in both blocks ... although some sessions failed the first criterion and were discarded (p > 0.05 for 4/55 sessions)
outcomes.notes: None of the 54 analysed sessions (55 less the catch-trial session) fails the two-sided binomial test in either block (largest p 0.039; lowest performance 59.6%), so the bound of at most 4 failures holds, and reading (b) of the session count (no analysed session fails) holds too. Median trials per session 736 under reading (a), trials performed, and 699.5 under reading (b), munged and nonrandom dropped; both within 698 +/- 69.8. Median performance over sessions is within 8.5 points of 85% in both blocks for CR20B (87.6, 81.6), CR21A (88.3, 90.6) and CR24A (87.2, 86.2). The paper's four discarded sessions are not in the data set.
deviations: The best rat's typical performance is read, as the claims file's check notes, as the median over a rat's sessions; the value recorded is CR20B localization, the first rat meeting the criterion.

outcomes.statement: Performance is typically better on go trials than on nogo trials.
outcomes.source: Results, A Novel Behavioral Task for Rodents, paragraph 2; Figure S1A
outcomes.quote: Performance was typically better on go trials than on nogo trials
outcomes.notes: Go performance exceeds nogo performance in 12 of 12 rat and block pairs (differences 6.8 to 30.6 points).

outcomes.statement: After each block change rats switch rapidly to the new target; performance dips briefly during the cue trials at the start of a block and recovers within a few trials.
outcomes.source: Results, A Novel Behavioral Task for Rodents, paragraph 2; Figure 2D legend
outcomes.quote: After each block change, rats rapidly and correctly switched to selecting the new target sound ... Performance briefly dips during cue trials at the beginning of a block but recovers within a few trials
outcomes.notes: Hit fraction on the first trial of the block is 0.560 (localization) and 0.496 (pitch discrimination), below the non-cue means of 0.833 and 0.785; both reach the mean at the sixth trial of the block, within 10. The within-5 variant does not hold in either block. The fold is aligned with the blocks: positions 1 to 20, 21 to 80, 81 to 100 and 101 to 160 hold only block values 1, 2, 3 and 4, and no position holds two block values.

outcomes.statement: The median intertrial interval is 4.0 s (interquartile range 2.7 to 5.3 s).
outcomes.source: Results, Within-Trial Timescale of the Encoding of the Selection Rule, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: Across the data set, the median intertrial interval was 4.0 s (interquartile range, 2.7-5.3 s)
outcomes.notes: Reading (a), consecutive stimulus onsets over the 47 sessions with included units: median 3.99 s, IQR 2.65 to 5.23 s (35741 intervals). Reading (b), center-poke starts, gives 3.99, 2.65 and 5.23 s. Dropping munged trials changes the values by at most 0.01 s.
deviations: Intervals are taken between consecutive rows of trial_timings, including intervals that span a munged or skipped trial; the variant with munged trials dropped is shown.

outcomes.statement: In the hold period of correct trials, 63% (76 of 121) of mPFC neurons individually encode the selection rule; 36 prefer localization and 40 pitch discrimination, and neither preference is significantly more common.
outcomes.source: Results, Anticipatory Neuronal Activity in mPFC and A1 Encodes the Selection Rule, paragraph 3; Figure 3C
outcomes.quote: population of mPFC neurons, 63% (76/121) of the neurons individually and significantly encoded the selection rule during the hold period (Figure 3C). Of these, 36 neurons preferred (i.e., fired ... more during) localization and 40 preferred pitch discrimination; neither preference was significantly more common (binomial test, p > 0.05)
outcomes.notes: Reading (a), BH over all 220 units as the code: 76 of 121 mPFC units encode the rule, 36 prefer localization and 40 pitch discrimination, binomial p = 0.73. Reading (b), BH within region: 81, 37 and 44 (binomial p = 0.51), each within tolerance (44 at the edge of 40 +/- 4), so the claim holds under both readings. The paper's code is ported to Python 3; R's wilcox.test (exact=FALSE) is reproduced with scipy's normal approximation with continuity correction, and R's p.adjust BH with statsmodels.

outcomes.statement: In the hold period of correct trials, 36% (36 of 99) of A1 neurons encode the selection rule; 13 prefer localization and 23 pitch discrimination, and neither preference is significantly more common.
outcomes.source: Results, Anticipatory Neuronal Activity in mPFC and A1 Encodes the Selection Rule, paragraph 4; Figure 4C
outcomes.quote: Across our recorded population, 36% (36/99) of A1 neurons encoded selection rule. As with mPFC, neither population was significantly larger (13 preferring localization, 23 preferring pitch discrimination; binomial test, p > 0.05)
outcomes.notes: Reading (a): 36 of 99 A1 units, 13 localization and 23 pitch discrimination, binomial p = 0.13. Reading (b): 35, 12 and 23 (p = 0.09), also within tolerance.

outcomes.statement: In A1, rule encoding is not significantly more common among stimulus-responsive neurons (14 of 49) than among nonresponsive ones (22 of 50).
outcomes.source: Results, Anticipatory Neuronal Activity in mPFC and A1 Encodes the Selection Rule, paragraph 4
outcomes.quote: Rule encoding was not significantly more widespread in either stimulus-responsive (14/49) or nonresponsive (22/50) neurons (p > 0.05, Fisher's exact test)
outcomes.notes: 14 of 49 responsive and 22 of 50 nonresponsive A1 units encode the rule; Fisher's exact p = 0.144, odds ratio 0.51. With M4 reading (b) (recomputed responsiveness, a variant) the test also finds no difference (p = 0.39 and 0.21).

outcomes.statement: Among rule-encoding neurons, the median increase in hold-period firing rate in the preferred block is 74.7% in mPFC and 99.7% in A1.
outcomes.source: Results, Anticipatory Neuronal Activity in mPFC and A1 Encodes the Selection Rule, paragraph 5
outcomes.quote: among rule-encoding neurons, the median increase in firing rate during the preferred block was 74.7% in mPFC and 99.7% in A1
outcomes.notes: Median increase 74.7% over 76 mPFC units and 99.8% over 36 A1 units.

outcomes.statement: Two simultaneously recorded mPFC units encode the rule with opposite preferences; one fires 12.1 Hz in localization against 7.2 Hz in pitch discrimination (483 and 295 trials), the other 5.4 Hz in pitch discrimination against 2.7 Hz in localization, both p < 0.001.
outcomes.source: Figure 3A and 3B legends
outcomes.quote: During the hold period (gray), the firing rate is significantly (p < 0.001, unpaired Mann-Whitney U-test) higher on localization (mean 12.1 Hz, n = 483) than on pitch discrimination (mean 7.2 Hz, n = 295) trials ... The hold period firing rate is significantly (p < 0.001) higher on pitch discrimination (mean 5.4 Hz) than on localization (mean 2.7 Hz) trials
outcomes.notes: Unit 257: 12.07 Hz localization against 7.19 Hz pitch discrimination over 483 and 295 trials, p = 2.0e-21. Unit 259: 5.41 Hz pitch discrimination against 2.66 Hz localization, p = 2.8e-13.

outcomes.statement: Two simultaneously recorded A1 units encode the rule; one fires 8.0 Hz in localization against 4.8 Hz in pitch discrimination, the other 10.1 Hz in pitch discrimination against 2.0 Hz in localization, both p < 0.001.
outcomes.source: Figure 4A and 4B legends
outcomes.quote: An example A1 neuron that responds significantly more (p < 0.001) during localization (8.0 Hz, n = 312 trials) than during pitch discrimination (4.8 Hz, n = 253) ... Simultaneously recorded A1 neuron that significantly (p < 0.001) prefers pitch discrimination (10.1 Hz, n = 312 trials) over localization (2.0 Hz, n = 253)
outcomes.notes: Re-run after a reader's answer (questions/crcns-pfc-1.yaml). The claims file first named unit A and unit B by the code's figure index (4A unit 612, 4B unit 712 of CR20B_120602), and under that assignment none of the four rates was within tolerance, so the outcome was not_reproduced. The reader amended the criterion to identify the units by preference, as the Figure 4 legends do, with the index's panel assignment not binding. Of the pair, unit 712 prefers localization and is unit A (8.01 Hz in localization against 4.76 Hz in pitch discrimination), and unit 612 is unit B (10.07 Hz in pitch discrimination against 2.00 Hz in localization). All four rates are within 10% of the expected values, the unadjusted Mann-Whitney p are 3.9e-12 (712) and 2.4e-62 (612), both below 0.001, and both units have 312 localization and 253 pitch discrimination trials, which matches the pair 312 and 253 in the 4A legend's assignment of the blocks. The assignment found swaps the code's index (712 is 4A, 612 is 4B).

outcomes.statement: In mPFC rule-encoding neurons, rule encoding is weakened on interference trials; the hold-period response on interference trials is higher than on correct trials in the non-preferred block and lower in the preferred block (57 neurons).
outcomes.source: Results, Error Trial Analysis, paragraph 2; Figure 3D legend
outcomes.quote: in mPFC, the encoding of selection rule was significantly weakened on interference trials, as compared with correct trials ... The population response on interference trials is significantly increased during the nonpreferred block and decreased during the preferred block (n = 57 neurons, paired Mann-Whitney test)
outcomes.notes: 57 mPFC units with at least 3 trials in each category. Interference minus hit, non-preferred block +3.42 Hz (37 of 57 higher, signed-rank p = 0.0012); preferred block -2.05 Hz (16 of 57 higher, p = 0.0011).

outcomes.statement: In A1 rule-encoding neurons the rule encoding is reversed on interference trials; the hold-period response on interference trials is greater in the non-preferred block than in the preferred block (16 neurons).
outcomes.source: Results, Error Trial Analysis, paragraph 2; Figure 4D legend
outcomes.quote: The population response on interference trials (orange bars) is significantly greater during the nonpreferred block than during the preferred block (p < 0.01, n = 16 neurons, paired Mann-Whitney U-test)
outcomes.notes: 16 A1 units. Interference in the non-preferred block exceeds interference in the preferred block by 4.55 Hz (14 of 16 units), signed-rank p = 0.0011, below 0.01.

outcomes.statement: In rule-encoding neurons of both regions, hold-period activity does not differ between correct go, correct nogo and go-on-nogo error trials within a block, while interference trials differ from all other trial types.
outcomes.source: Figure S2C and S3C legends
outcomes.quote: There is no significant difference in the hold period activity between correct go, correct nogo, and incorrect go-on-nogo trials ... However, there is a significant difference between interference trials and all other trial types in that block ... However, there is no difference between the other trial types, regardless of whether the rat performed a go or nogo response
outcomes.notes: 57 mPFC and 16 A1 units with at least 3 trials in each of the 8 categories. In each region all six comparisons among correct go, correct nogo and go-on-nogo errors have Bonferroni-corrected p = 1, and all six comparisons of interference with another category have corrected p below 0.05 (0.0029 to 0.035).

outcomes.statement: Across rule-encoding neurons in both regions, the hold-period rate is significantly above the spontaneous rate in the preferred block and significantly below it in the non-preferred block.
outcomes.source: Results, Within-Trial Timescale of the Encoding of the Selection Rule, paragraph 4; Figures S2F and S3F
outcomes.quote: across the population of rule-encoding neurons, the firing rate was significantly higher than spontaneous during the preferred block and significantly lower than spontaneous during the nonpreferred block
outcomes.notes: In all four region and preference groups (mPFC 36 and 40, A1 13 and 23 units) the preferred-block rate is above and the non-preferred-block rate below the spontaneous rate, signed-rank p from 0.0001 to 0.025. The pooled variant gives p of 0.0002 or less in both regions.

outcomes.statement: The median rule-encoding unit first shows a significant block preference 0.55 s before the stimulus in A1 and 0.625 s before it in mPFC, so most develop it before the trial is initiated.
outcomes.source: Results, Within-Trial Timescale of the Encoding of the Selection Rule, paragraphs 1 and 2; Figures 5A and 5B
outcomes.quote: In A1, the median rule-encoding unit first developed a significant block preference 0.55 s prestimulus; in PFC, the median was 0.625 s prestimulus. Thus, the majority of ... neurons developed this property well before the rat initiated a trial by center-poking
outcomes.notes: With the code's smoother, median onset 0.550 s before stimulus in A1 (36 units) and 0.625 s in mPFC (76 units), for W = 3 s and W = 5 s alike; both above 0.35 s. With exact spike times in place of the code's grid (variant) the medians are 0.575 s and 0.750 s, the mPFC value outside tolerance. 7 mPFC and 2 A1 units have an onset although their bin before onset is not significant (main3.py marks them invalid, main4.py keeps them); their onsets are 0.05 and 0.15 s in A1 and 0 to 1.35 s in mPFC. Counting them as having no preference before the stimulus (onset 0) gives 0.550 s in A1 and 0.600 s in mPFC, within tolerance; leaving them out gives 0.650 s in both regions, outside tolerance in A1. The outcome rests on keeping them (see deviations).
deviations: Assumed: the median is taken over all rule-encoding units, including the 7 mPFC and 2 A1 units that have no significant interval containing the bin just before onset, each with the onset main4.py gives it. The criterion defines the interval as the run that contains the bin just before onset, which these units lack, but also takes the median over units as main4.py does. The paper speaks of "the median rule-encoding unit" (Results, Within-Trial Timescale of the Encoding of the Selection Rule, paragraph 2), and Figure 5C gives n = 76 and 36 rule-encoding neurons, which supports a median over all of them. Leaving the units out fails in A1 (0.650 s); a question for a reader is in questions/crcns-pfc-1.yaml.

The smoothing follows kkpandas.base.GaussianSmoother as 5-2-timecourse_exemplars/main1.py and main2.py use it: each spike is moved to the nearest 50 ms sample point and a Gaussian of one sample s.d., truncated at 3 s.d. and normalized to sum to one, is added there (modules/kkpandas/base.py, modules/DiscreteAnalyze/PointProc.py). The paper says only that spike trains were smoothed with a 50 ms Gaussian; the result in mPFC depends on this discretization.
R's wilcox.test with fix_float=10000 (rounding of values) is not reproduced; scipy's test is applied to the smoothed values directly.

outcomes.statement: The population activity of rule-encoding neurons in their preferred block ramps up before the stimulus and is significantly elevated earlier in mPFC (from 2.7 s before stimulus onset) than in A1 (from 0.88 s).
outcomes.source: Results, Within-Trial Timescale of the Encoding of the Selection Rule, paragraph 3; Figure 5C legend
outcomes.quote: The PFC population increases its response earlier (first significantly activated 2.7 s before stimulus onset) than the A1 population (first significantly activated 0.88 s before stimulus onset)
outcomes.notes: First significant bin with positive mean, 2.725 s before onset in mPFC (76 units) and 0.875 s in A1 (36 units); mPFC earlier. Smoothing with exact spike times gives the same bins.

outcomes.statement: In the preferred block, after the rat leaves the center port, the population rate of rule-encoding neurons stays above baseline for several seconds on nogo trials and falls below baseline on go trials, in both mPFC and A1.
outcomes.source: Results, Encoding of Behavioral Choice, paragraph 1; Figure 5D legend
outcomes.quote: On nogo trials (gray), the firing rate remained elevated above baseline for at least several seconds ... On go trials, the firing rate was suppressed below baseline as the rat moved to the choice port and consumed a reward
outcomes.notes: Reading (a): mPFC nogo +0.437 (p < 0.0001), go -0.163 (p = 0.021); A1 nogo +0.264 (p = 0.0007), go -0.421 (p = 0.0001). Reading (b) holds in mPFC (96% of nogo bins and 56% of go bins from 0.5 to 3 s significant in the claimed direction) but not in A1 (nogo 28%). The outcome rests on reading (a); in A1 the support for a nogo rate elevated for several seconds is weaker than in mPFC.

outcomes.statement: Auditory-responsive neurons are significantly rarer in mPFC (31 of 121) than in A1 (49 of 99).
outcomes.source: Results, Changes in Baseline Activity Correlate with Changes in Evoked Activity, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: Auditory-responsive neurons in mPFC were significantly rarer (mPFC, 31/121; A1, 49/99; p < 0.001, Fisher's exact test) than in A1
outcomes.notes: Reading (a): 31 of 121 mPFC and 49 of 99 A1 units responsive, Fisher's exact p = 0.0004. These counts are the code's unit table. Reading (b), recomputed from the spikes as the Supplement describes (a variant): 46 of 121 and 61 of 99 (p = 0.00067), or 46 and 58 when windows that run to the end of the 50 ms are excluded (p = 0.0028); outside tolerance, so the claim holds under reading (a) only. The outcome reproduces the code's tabulation, not the classification from the spikes.
deviations: Reading (b) uses choices the Supplement leaves open: all trials of all stimuli, 0 to 50 ms after onset, p < 0.05 uncorrected per bin, the code's discretized 1 ms smoother on a 0.5 ms grid; the 4 atypical units the Supplement discards cannot be identified and are not discarded.

outcomes.statement: Onset responses are stronger in auditory-responsive A1 neurons than in mPFC neurons, 0.12 against 0.02 extra spikes per trial (median) and 209% against 171% of baseline.
outcomes.source: Figure S5C and S5D legends
outcomes.quote: The responses are significantly stronger in A1 neurons (median: 0.12 spikes) than in PFC neurons (median: 0.02 spikes), p < 0.001, unpaired Mann-Whitney U-test ... Again the responses are stronger in A1 neurons (median: 209% of baseline) than in PFC neurons (median: 171% of baseline), p < 0.001, unpaired Mann-Whitney U-test
outcomes.notes: Medians A1 0.116 and mPFC 0.019 extra spikes per trial (Mann-Whitney p = 1.3e-09), A1 209.1% and mPFC 170.7% of baseline (p = 0.00061), over 49 and 31 units. Under M4 reading (b), a variant, A1 is also stronger (0.064 against 0.005 extra spikes, 198% against 145%).

outcomes.statement: The median response latency of auditory-responsive mPFC neurons is slightly but significantly longer than in A1, 19.75 against 16.75 ms.
outcomes.source: Results, Changes in Baseline Activity Correlate with Changes in Evoked Activity, paragraph 1; Figure S5E legend
outcomes.quote: Their median response latency was also significantly longer, though only slightly (19.75 ms versus 16.75 ms in A1; Figure S5E) ... though only slightly. p < 0.05, unpaired Mann-Whitney U-test
outcomes.notes: Median latency 19.75 ms in mPFC and 16.75 ms in A1, Mann-Whitney p = 0.010. Under M4 reading (b), a variant, the medians are 16.38 and 16.25 ms and do not differ (p = 0.41), so the result rests on the code's response windows.

outcomes.statement: Across auditory-responsive neurons, the change in hold-period rate between blocks correlates with the change in evoked rate, in A1 (43 neurons, trend slope close to 1) and in mPFC (17 neurons), p < 0.001 in each.
outcomes.source: Results, Changes in Baseline Activity Correlate with Changes in Evoked Activity, paragraph 2; Figure 6C and 6D legends
outcomes.quote: For A1 neurons (n = 43), increased anticipatory firing during one block significantly correlated (p < 0.001) with increased evoked responses during the same block ... The slope of the trend line is close to 1 ... but for auditory-responsive mPFC neurons (n = 17). Again, the change in anticipatory activity across neurons correlated closely with the change in evoked response (p < 0.001)
outcomes.notes: After the weak-response filter (6 A1 and 14 mPFC units dropped), 43 A1 and 17 mPFC units. A1 slope 0.977 (95% CI 0.478 to 1.477, contains 1), r = 0.525, p = 0.0003; mPFC slope 1.455, r = 0.848, p = 1.7e-05.
deviations: The bootstrap draws (10000, seed fixed) differ from the paper's, so the evoked change of each unit differs by sampling error.

outcomes.statement: After subtracting each block's baseline, only 6 of 43 A1 neurons (14%) change their evoked response significantly between blocks, 4 of the 6 from one rat (Rat 1), with higher rates in pitch discrimination.
outcomes.source: Results, Changes in Baseline Activity Correlate with Changes in Evoked Activity, paragraph 2; Supplemental Experimental Procedures, Changes in magnitude of evoked response not explained by changes in baseline
outcomes.quote: we found very little evidence of any block-specific change in evoked firing rate ... We found that a small population (6/43, or 14%) of A1 neurons increased their evoked response significantly ... these neurons were predominantly (4/6) observed in a single animal (Rat 1)
outcomes.notes: 6 of 43 A1 units significant after BH within region; 4 from CR12B (Rat 1), all 4 higher in pitch discrimination; the other 2 (CR17B) higher in localization. Unadjusted variant 12 of 43, 9 from CR12B. mPFC 1 of 17. The outcome rests on the code's BH correction: the unadjusted count (12, 6 of the 9 CR12B units higher in pitch discrimination) fails the criterion. Two further bootstrap seeds give the same 6 units after BH (4 CR12B, all higher in pitch discrimination); the next unit in rank has adjusted p = 0.063.
deviations: The code's bootstrap draws the same number of trials for both blocks (it reuses the localization labels for the pitch discrimination draw); this is kept.

outcomes.statement: Sound identity is decoded more accurately from A1 ensembles (21 ensembles, 49 neurons) than from mPFC ensembles (17 ensembles, 31 neurons), but for neither sound nor region is decoding better in one block than the other.
outcomes.source: Results, Changes in Baseline Activity Correlate with Changes in Evoked Activity, paragraph 3; Figure 6E legend
outcomes.quote: It could be decoded significantly more accurately (p < 0.001 for the main effect of brain region) using A1 responses (n = 21 ensembles of 49 neurons total) than using mPFC responses (n = 17 ensembles of 31 neurons total). However, for both sounds and both brain regions, the decoding was not significantly more accurate during either pitch discrimination (red) or localization (blue) trials (p > 0.05 for each pair of bars using a paired t test)

statistics.test: three-way ANOVA on brain region, target sound and block

statistics.about: localization against pitch discrimination, each region and sound

outcomes.notes: 21 A1 ensembles of 49 units and 17 mPFC ensembles of 31 units. Region main effect F = 39.3, p < 0.001, A1 higher (mean score 0.570 against 0.521). The four paired t-tests between blocks give adjusted p 0.35 to 0.59 (unadjusted 0.088 to 0.59). Leave-one-out variant: region F = 21.6, p < 0.001; block comparisons adjusted p 0.57 to 0.83. The in-sample score's chance level, from 100 label shuffles per score, is about 0.54 in A1 and 0.52 in mPFC; A1 scores exceed it by 0.031 (paired t p = 1.6e-06), mPFC scores by 0.003 (p = 0.094), so the mPFC block comparisons are made on scores near chance.
deviations: scikit-learn's LogisticRegression with the liblinear solver (the default of the code's version) and class_weight balanced (the code's 'auto').

outcomes.statement: There is no correlation between a neuron's change in anticipatory activity and its tuning for the noise burst or the warble, in A1 or mPFC.
outcomes.source: Results, Changes in Baseline Activity Correlate with Changes in Evoked Activity, paragraph 4; Figure S5F and S5G legends
outcomes.quote: we did not observe any correlation between each neuron's change in anticipatory activity and its tuning for the stimuli
outcomes.notes: 23 A1 and 9 mPFC units pass the code's minimums (10 evoked spikes, 25 cue trials per block). The four regressions give r = 0.156, 0.037 (A1) and -0.214, 0.513 (mPFC), p = 0.48, 0.87, 0.58, 0.16. The mPFC test rests on 9 units. With 9 mPFC units only |r| of 0.82 or more is detectable with 80% power (0.56 for 23 A1 units); the 95% intervals of r are -0.77 to 0.52 and -0.23 to 0.88 in mPFC.

outcomes.statement: No stimulus pair shows a greater change in evoked response between blocks than the others, with or without baseline subtraction, and in absolute value; and no stimulus pair's change differs from zero.
outcomes.source: Results, Changes in Baseline Activity Correlate with Changes in Evoked Activity, paragraph 4; Figure S5H and S5I legends
outcomes.quote: A one-way Kruskal-Wallis test revealed no significant difference between the stimulus pairs ... We found no significant difference from zero for any individual stimulus pair
outcomes.notes: None of 24 tests has p < 0.05: Kruskal-Wallis p from 0.061 (A1, absolute raw) to 0.92; Wilcoxon against zero, adjusted p from 0.12 to 0.99 (49 A1 and 31 mPFC units).

outcomes.statement: Anticipatory firing rate does not correlate with reaction time or movement time; few neurons correlate individually and the mean correlation does not differ from zero.
outcomes.source: Discussion, The Potential Roles of Motor Planning and Posture, paragraph 3; Figures S2G, S2H, S3G, S3H legends
outcomes.quote: we did not observe any correlation between the anticipatory firing rate and the reaction or movement time

statistics.about: mean of the correlation coefficients against zero

outcomes.notes: Mean r against 0, one-sample t-test p from 0.052 (A1 localization reaction time, mean r 0.016) to 0.90 over the eight region, block and measure sets; 0 to 5 units individually significant after BH. Movement time from center-port exit (variant) gives p from 0.49 to 0.98. One unit-block fit for movement time had a constant count and was dropped. The 95% intervals of the mean r lie within -0.03 to +0.04 for all eight sets; A1 localization reaction time -0.0001 to 0.031.

outcomes.statement: The rat's head angle during the center poke differs between blocks by about 30 degrees, 26.9, 36.6 and 24.1 degrees in the three scored sessions.
outcomes.source: Results, Potential Role of Posture, paragraph 1; Figure S2I legend; Supplemental Experimental Procedures, Video analysis of preparatory head positioning
outcomes.quote: differs by approximately 30 degrees between blocks ... The mean difference between blocks was 26.9, 36.6, and 24.1 degrees in each of the three analyzed sessions
outcomes.notes: Localization minus pitch discrimination mean head angle: -26.92 (CR24A_121022), -36.60 (CR20B_120602) and -24.07 degrees (CR17B_110803), on 768, 565 and 207 trials of the hold analysis.

outcomes.statement: For most rule-encoding neurons, block explains far more of the hold-period variance than head angle; the median fraction explained by block is 94.1% in mPFC and 83.0% in A1 (head angle 5.9% and 17.0%), and only 3 of 16 mPFC and 1 A1 neuron are mostly explained by head angle.
outcomes.source: Figures S2K, S2L, S3K, S3L legends; Supplemental Experimental Procedures, Video analysis, Results
outcomes.quote: Only three out of 16 bars are more than 50% black ... most of the variance (median: 94.1%) is explained by block; the small amount that remains is explained by head angle (median: 5.9%) ... Only one bar is more than 50% black ... most of the variance (median: 83.0%) is explained by block; the small amount that remains is explained by head angle (median: 17.0%)
outcomes.notes: mPFC (16 units): median FEV block 94.1%, head angle 5.9%, 3 units above 50% head angle. A1: one of 8 units has overall F p = 0.129 and is left out; of the 7, median 83.0% and 17.0%, one unit above 50%.

outcomes.statement: On posture-equalized trials the rule encoding persists; its population spread (0.471 in mPFC, 0.318 in A1) exceeds that of shuffles (p < 0.005), and only 1 of 16 mPFC and 0 of 8 A1 cells switch preferred block (binomial p = 0.0005 and 0.008).
outcomes.source: Results, Potential Role of Posture, paragraph 2; Figures S2M, S2O, S3M, S3O; Supplemental Experimental Procedures, Posture equalization by trial selection
outcomes.quote: The PRE was 0.471 in PFC and 0.318 in A1 on the posture-equalized trials; the fraction of shuffles that yielded a greater PRE was <0.005 in both brain regions ... In fact we observed that only 1/16 PFC cells and 0/8 A1 cells switch their preferred block after posture equalization. The p-value (two-tailed binomial test) of this result is 0.008 for A1 and 0.0005 in PFC
outcomes.notes: Posture-equalized trials per block 103 (CR24A), 33 (CR20B) and 39 (CR17B). PRE (MAD about the median, statsmodels' robust.mad) 0.471 in mPFC and 0.318 in A1; shuffle p = 0.0001 in both. 1 of 16 mPFC and 0 of 8 A1 cells switch, binomial p = 0.0005 and 0.0078. The uncentered MAD (variant, which the code's comment says its statsmodels computed) gives 0.327 and 0.343.
deviations: 10000 shuffles with a fixed seed of their own; the shuffle p is limited to 1/10000 resolution.

outcomes.statement: The mean magnitude of rule encoding is not significantly altered on posture-equalized trials, in mPFC or A1.
outcomes.source: Figures S2N and S3N legends; Supplemental Experimental Procedures, Posture equalization by trial selection
outcomes.quote: we found that the mean magnitude of rule-encoding was not significantly altered by postural equalization
outcomes.notes: Signed-rank test of |log10 ratio| on posture-equalized against other trials: p = 0.059 in mPFC (16 cells; 0.308 against 0.418) and 0.141 in A1 (8 cells; 0.218 against 0.401). The magnitude is lower on posture-equalized trials in both regions, without significance. The code's per-preference variant gives p from 0.09 to 0.36. 95% intervals of the mean change in |log10 ratio| -0.237 to +0.016 (mPFC) and -0.442 to +0.076 (A1); lower on posture-equalized trials in 11 of 16 and 6 of 8 cells. The test of absence has little power.

outcomes.statement: Electrical disruption of mPFC impairs performance; across sessions the impairment is significant in pitch discrimination for all three rats and in localization for two of three.
outcomes.source: Results, Disruption of mPFC Significantly Impairs Task Performance, paragraph 2; Figure 7A
outcomes.quote: This impairment was significant across sessions (p < 0.05, binomial test on the number of impaired sessions) during pitch discrimination for all (three of three) rats and during localization for most (two of three) rats

statistics.test: binomial test on the number of impaired sessions

outcomes.notes: Sessions with control above disruption: pitch discrimination 6 of 6 (Z1, p = 0.031), 8 of 8 (Z2, p = 0.0078), 8 of 8 (Z3, p = 0.0078); localization 5 of 6 (Z1, p = 0.22), 8 of 8 and 8 of 8 (p = 0.0078). Session counts 6, 8 and 8. Dropping nonrandom trials changes nothing.

outcomes.statement: Disruption impairs nogo trials in particular; every rat is significantly impaired on nogo trials in one block or the other, and Z2 also on localization go trials.
outcomes.source: Results, Disruption of mPFC Significantly Impairs Task Performance, paragraph 2; Figure 7C legend
outcomes.quote: All rats were significantly impaired on nogo trials during one block or the other. One rat (Z2) also showed a significant impairment on localization go trials

statistics.test: binomial test on number of impaired sessions

outcomes.notes: Significant nogo impairment: Z1 pitch discrimination (6 of 6, p = 0.031), Z2 pitch discrimination (8 of 8, p = 0.0078), Z3 localization (8 of 8, p = 0.0078). The only significant go impairment is Z2 localization (8 of 8, p = 0.0078).

outcomes.statement: Rats perform as well when the distractor is replaced by a novel neutral sound as on standard trials, so they select the target and do not memorize the four stimulus pairs.
outcomes.source: Figure S1B and S1C legends
outcomes.quote: The rats perform just as well on catch trials as on standard trials (Fisher's Exact Test on the trial outcomes, p > 0.05 in all cases)
outcomes.notes: All eight Fisher's exact tests give p > 0.05 (0.11 to 1.0). Catch performance 0.75 to 1.00 against standard 0.79 to 0.98. CR20B's file holds one session (390 trials, 51 catch); CR21A's 663 trials (99 catch).

outcomes.statement: In the network model with 320 neurons, a task signal alone lets the network perform above 80% correct with a sensory signal-to-noise ratio as low as 0.0625, and 100% at an SNR of 0.25 for virtually any positive task signal.
outcomes.source: Results, A Simulated Network Model, paragraph 3; Figure 8B legend
outcomes.quote: With 320 neurons, the network performs above 80% correct even with a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) as low as 0.0625 ... At the highest SNR of 0.25 (darkest trace), the model produces 100% correct responses for virtually any positive task switch signal
outcomes.notes: N = 320. At SNR 0.0625 (noise level 16) the best positive task signal gives 93.2% correct in task 1 and in task 2, above 80%. At SNR 0.25 task 1 is at least 99% at every sampled task signal over noise from 0.32 to 10, which is 90% of Figure 8B's positive plotted axis (symlog, 8-1-model/main1.py set_xlim) and 97% of the linear range 0 to 10, and at 38 of 40 (95%) positive gains of the code's narrow linear sweep (gains 0.25 to 20). Within the plotted range it is below 99% only for task signals under 0.3 times the noise, where task 1 performance runs from about 0.63 at the smallest gains to 0.988 at a gain of 1.194 (task signal / noise 0.30); above the plotted range it falls (0.52 at a gain of 84). Counted over the log-spaced broad gains, which crowd near zero, 25% of the positive gains reach 99% (30% within the plotted range). The SNR is 1 / noise level, the code's label (gain/noise with sensory gain 1); gain/sqrt(noise) does not give the printed grid.
deviations: Which positive task signals count is not stated. "Most positive task signals" is read as most of the range of task signals that Figure 8B plots, the figure the quote describes; the narrow linear sweep agrees. Counted per log-spaced sample of the broad sweep the second condition would not hold; both counts are shown.

findings.statement: The spike files hold 2977 sorted clusters, good units and bad clusters alike, with nothing in the data set that says which are the 220 well-sorted units the paper analysed, or gives their auditory response class and window. These come only from metadata/unit_db.csv in the paper's code repository; the scripts that made the table are not published.

The auditory response classes of unit_db.csv apply rules the paper does not state (classes too brief, lasts to end, lasts too long). Recomputing responsiveness as the Supplement describes gives 46 mPFC and 61 A1 responsive units in place of the paper's 31 and 49, and, of 67 units responsive under both, 17 whose window starts at a different time. Part of the difference is the table's unstated classes (units classed too brief, lasts too long or lasts to end are responsive when recomputed), and part the threshold and trial choices of the recomputation (6 units classed nothing become responsive, 13 classed responsive do not).

The spike files (*.kkp) and the miscellaneous pickles are pandas 0.10 pickles written under Python 2. Current pandas cannot open them (module pandas.core.index no longer exists); the descriptor's pandas.load no longer exists either. They can be read with a custom unpickler.

Two sessions, CR21A_120503_004 and CR21A_120504_004, hold a second spike file at the session level besides klusters0/. It has the same spike times, but its column is named spike_time, tetrode groups run 0 to 7 in place of 1 to 8, and the unit numbers differ, so the descriptor's unit-number rule may assign units differently. The descriptor does not mention these files.

The data descriptor names the stimulus column stimulus_name; the files call it stim_name. The descriptor numbers the stimuli starting with le_lc_go as 1; in the files le_lc_go is 3, ri_lc_no 4, lo_pc_go 1 and hi_pc_no 2.

Three sessions (CR20B_120613, CR21A_120502, CR21A_120506) have no spike file; their klusters0/ holds a README.txt, where the descriptor says the directory is empty. The data set holds the 55 sessions the paper reports after its four discarded sessions; the discarded ones are not in it.

metadata/figures_generated_by_each_script.csv names CR20B_120602_001_behaving-612 as Figure 4A and -712 as Figure 4B. The legends' values fit the reverse: 712 prefers localization (8.01 against 4.76 Hz) and 612 pitch discrimination (10.07 against 2.00 Hz).

The Figure 4B legend gives the trial counts of the simultaneously recorded pair with the blocks swapped (pitch discrimination 312, localization 253) relative to the 4A legend (localization 312, pitch discrimination 253); the data have 312 localization and 253 pitch discrimination trials for both units.

For the single-unit onsets of Figures 5A and 5B (fig5ab-single-unit-onset), 7 mPFC and 2 A1 rule-encoding units have no significant interval containing the bin just before stimulus onset. 5-2-timecourse_exemplars/main3.py marks them invalid but main4.py keeps them in the median, and the paper does not say how such units count. Kept, the medians are 0.550 s (A1) and 0.625 s (mPFC), the paper's values; counted with onset 0 they are 0.550 and 0.600 s; left out, 0.650 s in both. Were these units included in "the median rule-encoding unit", and with what onset?

3-5-vidtrack/main5.py says statsmodels' stand_mad does not subtract the median, but the paper's PRE values (0.471 and 0.318) are reproduced exactly by the MAD about the median; the uncentered MAD gives 0.327 and 0.343.

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebook)
verifications.reviewed: Round 1. The first executed notebook with the conclusion cells and the summary removed, the helper module and the claims file, with the paper. The verifier read four scripts of the paper's code at commit 390b608 and tested helper functions on synthetic inputs. It gave its own outcome for each of the 35 claims; 34 agree with the record, and for fig8-model it gave reproduced where the record had partially_reproduced. The revision added the outputs it asked for, moved four conclusions out of section headers that the handover had kept, added the notebook header and changed fig8-model to reproduced.

disagreements.reason: At N = 320 and SNR 0.0625 the best performance is 0.932 in both tasks. At SNR 0.25 performance is ≥ 0.99 for every task signal/noise value from 0.3 to 10, but only for 25 to 30% of the log-spaced gain samples. The broad gains, x = gain/noise and a symlog x axis limited to (-1, 10) are the code's choices. The claim passes when counted over the plotted axis and fails when counted over sampled gains, because the log-spaced samples crowd near zero; above the plot range performance falls to 0.5. Reproduced rests on the axis reading, which matches Figure 8B; the claims file does not settle which reading is meant (problem 2). Performance on the narrow linear gains at SNR 0.25 was not shown.

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebook)
verifications.reviewed: Round 2. The full executed notebook after the round-1 revision, the helper module, the claims file and the attempt record, with the paper. The verifier agreed with all 35 outcomes, for fig5ab-single-unit-onset only under a reading it asked to be marked as assumed, and listed sentences the numbers do not support in cells 19, 33, 111, 123, the summary and the README. It did not read the code's scripts beyond the four of round 1 and re-ran nothing. The revision corrected those sentences, marked fig5ab-single-unit-onset as assumed and asked a reader how the criterion counts its units without an interval; no outcome changed.

entries.name: rodgers-2014
entries.title: Task switching in rat prefrontal and auditory cortex (Rodgers and DeWeese 2014)
entries.description: Tests the findings of Rodgers and DeWeese (2014) on CRCNS data set pfc-1, which holds the spike times and trial tables of 55 sessions of six rats performing an auditory stimulus selection task, with units in medial prefrontal cortex and primary auditory cortex, and the data of the paper's disruption, catch-trial, video-tracking and network-model analyses. It covers behaviour, the encoding of the selection rule before the stimulus, error trials, its time course, evoked responses and decoding, head posture, mPFC disruption and the model. The units analysed and their auditory response windows come from the paper's code repository.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Rodgers and DeWeese (2014) from CRCNS pfc-1
